column4: 80:19 says “خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ” of the human being: creation followed by measured determination, the same sequence as the source-section roots خ ل ق and ق د ر.
80:20 continues “ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ”: after creation and measure, the way is made easy. This directly joins the source-section roots ق د ر and ي س ر as measure followed by facilitated direction.
25:2 says God created everything and “فَقَدَّرَهُۥ تَقْدِيرًا.” The source-section’s craft reading of خَلَقَ as measuring before cutting makes the verse’s creation-with-measure sequence concrete.
54:49 says “إِنَّا كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَٰهُ بِقَدَرٍۢ”: everything created by measure, directly matching the source-section’s root ق د ر and its claim that every thing has an extent and term.

82:7 says God “خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ,” creating, proportioning, and balancing the human. Its sequence closely echoes the source-section’s خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ and the straightening of a shaped object.

Moses answers Pharaoh that the Lord “أَعْطَىٰ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلْقَهُۥ ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ”: each thing receives its created form and then guidance. This states the source-section’s movement from making a thing fit to directing it.
Abraham says of God, “ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَنِى فَهُوَ يَهْدِينِ.” The source-section cites this same pairing of creation and guidance, here spoken by Abraham as his account of dependence on his Lord.
91:7 swears by the soul and the One who “سَوَّىٰهَا.” This is the source-section’s root س و ي in the concrete scene of a proportioned creature.

91:8 says the soul was inspired with its wickedness and piety; after 91:7’s proportioning, it gives a moral direction to the formed soul, completing the source-section’s claim that what is made is also turned toward a way.
91:9 says “قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّىٰهَا.” Its success and purification join the source-section’s mention of the successful person in 87:14 to the outcome of a rightly directed life.

91:10 says the one who buries the soul fails, the reversal of 91:9’s purified soul and of the source section’s successful outcome; it makes the measure-and-guidance image a fork with contrary results.
76:3 says God guided the human to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful. The source-section’s arrow-point gloss for ه د ي becomes a path with two possible responses.
3:6 says God forms people in their mothers’ wombs as He wills. This is a bodily instance of the source-section’s making and fitting a form to its intended measure.

23:12 begins the human’s making from an extract of clay. The source-section defines the root ر ب ب as bringing a thing state by state to completion; this is the first material stage in the adjacent account.
23:13 places the drop in a firm resting place, the next protected stage after 23:12 in the bodily sequence that illustrates the source-section’s definition of ر ب ب as gradual formation.

23:14 gives successive transformations of the drop and ends with another creation. This staged shaping gives a bodily counterpart to the source-section’s measured making and its definition of ر ب ب as bringing a thing to completion state by state.
16:68 says the Lord inspires the bee to make homes. It gives the source-section’s claim that the Maker also directs a creature a concrete case of guidance fitted to a creature’s work.

16:69 tells the bee to follow its Lord’s made-easy paths, from which healing drink comes. This makes the source-section’s guided direction and useful finished vessel perceptible in a creature’s directed route and beneficial product.
5:3 explicitly forbids “أَن تَسْتَقْسِمُوا۟ بِٱلْأَزْلَٰمِ,” seeking a share by divining arrows. It names the exact lot-arrow practice developed in the source-section and establishes its boundary.

5:90 names “ٱلْمَيْسِرُ” and “ٱلْأَزْلَٰمُ” together, then says “فَٱجْتَنِبُوهُ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ.” It directly connects the source-section’s lot-game to the roots of 87:11 (avoid) and 87:14 (succeed), while marking the game as forbidden.

2:219 asks about intoxicants and gambling and says their sin is greater than their benefit, “نَفْعِهِمَا.” It joins the source-section’s meysir game to its named root ن ف ع and distinguishes a game’s benefit from its greater harm.

3:44 recalls people casting their pens to decide who would care for Mary. It stages a lot that assigns a responsibility rather than a game’s prize, clarifying the boundary around the source-section’s arrow-drawn shares.
37:141 says Jonah “فَسَاهَمَ” and was among those who lost the lot. This is another concrete lot-drawing scene; its dangerous outcome differs from meysir’s distribution of a prize.

2:200 says the person who asks only for worldly good has no “خَلَاقٍ” in the Hereafter. The source-section identifies خَلَاق as a measured share, so this is a direct instance of a worldly choice leaving no afterlife share.

2:202 says those people have “نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟,” a share from what they earned. It clarifies the source-section’s contrast between a lot-won share and a share assigned in relation to what one has done.

9:69 says earlier communities enjoyed their “خَلَاقِهِمْ” and then their deeds came to nothing in this life and the next. The source-section’s dictionary sense of خَلَاق as a measured share makes their enjoyed portion a direct parallel with its warning about choosing worldly gain.

28:77 says to seek the Hereafter through what God gave and not forget one’s share of the world. It gives a specific alternative to the source-section’s warning about preferring this life over the more lasting one.

42:20 contrasts the harvest of the Hereafter with the harvest of this world and says the latter-seeker has no afterlife share. It makes the source-section’s choice between near and lasting shares explicit.
92:7 says “فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ,” easing a person toward ease. This repeats the source-section root ي س ر and specifies one direction of the life-choice its prose links to 87:8 and 87:16–17.

92:10 says a person may be eased toward hardship, using the source-section root ي س ر in a reversed outcome. It gives a specific opposite to 87:8’s ease and aligns with the source-section’s wretched person who avoids the reminder and enters fire.
92:12 says “إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَىٰ,” placing guidance upon God. This directly parallels the source-section’s ه د ي and its claim that making includes directing.
92:13 says the first life and the Hereafter belong to God. It grounds the source-section’s contrast between choosing the lowly near life and the more lasting afterlife in divine ownership of both.
92:14 warns of a blazing fire. It carries forward the source-section’s reference to entering the great fire in 87:12, with the next verses identifying who reaches it.
92:15 says only the most wretched will enter that fire. This gives a concrete counterpart to 87:11–12’s wretched person avoiding the reminder and entering fire.
92:16 characterizes that wretched person as one who denies and turns away. It specifies the refusal behind the avoidance named in 87:11, rather than leaving the fire as an unchosen fate.
92:17 says the most God-fearing will be kept away from the fire, the reverse outcome to 92:15 and to the source-section’s wretched person entering it.
92:18 describes the God-fearing person as giving wealth to purify himself. It gives a concrete counterpart to the source-section’s successful person who purifies himself in 87:14.

92:20 says the giver seeks “وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ.” The source-section links the highest meysir arrow, المُعَلَّى, to ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ in 87:1; this verse redirects the highest aim from a game’s share to the Lord.

92:21 promises that this person will be satisfied. It supplies the outcome of 92:18–20’s giving and seeking the Most High, a durable fulfillment alongside the source-section’s better, abiding Hereafter.

20:74 says the criminal in Hell will neither die there nor live. This is a precise parallel to the source surah’s next statement after the great fire in 87:12, and clarifies the fire’s boundary condition.
21:47 sets up just scales for Resurrection and says no soul will be wronged even by a mustard seed. Against the source-section’s chance-drawn shares, it marks the boundary of exact, just accounting.
101:6 asks whose scales are heavy. The source-section’s measured portion and the lot’s high share are recast as a measured deed-weight that determines the afterlife outcome.
101:7 says the heavy-scaled person will be in a pleasant life, completing the measured outcome begun in 101:6 and contrasting with the source section’s fire.
101:8 asks whose scales are light, the opposite measurement to 101:6 and a counterpart to the source-section’s wretched outcome.
101:9 identifies the light-scaled person’s destination as the abyss. It completes the scale’s contrary outcome in 101:8, as the source section pairs success with fire for the wretched.
23:102 says those whose scales are heavy are the successful. It joins measured weight to the success word that the source-section also connects to the share-arrow prohibition in 5:90.
23:103 says those whose scales are light have lost themselves and remain in Hell. It completes the opposite measured outcome and fire that frame the source-section’s choice of shares.
7:8 says weighing on that day is the truth and names the heavy scales. It links the source-section’s measured allotment to a just measure of deeds.
7:9 says those whose scales are light have lost themselves. Its reversed result clarifies that the source-section’s choice of share has consequences beyond a worldly draw.
99:7 says whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it. The tiny but exact weight makes the source-section’s measured allotment concrete in judgment.
99:8 applies the same atom-weight test to evil. It completes the balanced accounting of 99:7 and shows the boundary between the two outcomes.
6:160 assigns tenfold return for good and only its equivalent for evil. Its explicit ratio is a measured afterlife share, unlike a meysir prize decided by arrows.
65:3 says God has set “قَدْرًا” for everything and mentions provision from where one does not expect. It directly combines the source-section’s root ق د ر with an allotted provision.
13:8 says everything with God is by “مِقْدَارٍ” while describing what wombs carry. It gives the source-section’s measure-and-endpoint claim a specific created-life instance.
15:21 says nothing is sent down except by a known measure, in a passage about what is with God and what He sends. This concretizes the source-section’s measured making as measured provision.

42:27 says God sends provision down by measure as He wills, since unrestricted abundance would lead people to transgress. It connects the source-section’s measured share to provision and marks a limit on abundance.

43:32 says God apportioned people’s livelihoods and raised some over others in rank. It is a direct counterpart to the source-section’s shares, while locating their distribution in God’s ordering rather than a lottery.

16:71 names unequal provision among people and asks whether the favored will share it equally with those under their authority. This gives the source-section’s allotment of shares a concrete social consequence.
89:15 describes a person mistaking generous provision for honor. The next verse uses قَدَرَ for restricted provision, making this a concrete question of how an allotted share should be read.

89:16 says God “قَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ,” restricting provision, while the person mistakes this for humiliation. It completes 89:15 and clarifies that measured shares are not a simple worldly ranking.
4:7 gives men and women a prescribed share in inheritance. It contrasts a legally assigned portion with the arbitrary meysir shares in the source-section.
4:11 specifies children’s inheritance fractions as divine instruction. The fixed shares contrast with the chance allocation of the source-section’s lot game.
4:12 assigns spouses and relatives specific inheritance shares, another concrete contrast between measured allotment and game-drawn shares.
4:13 calls the inheritance rules “حُدُودُ ٱللَّهِ” and promises success to those who obey. It completes the share assignments of 4:11–12 as divinely set limits.
4:14 warns against crossing those limits and names the Fire. It supplies the boundary and consequence for the measured shares immediately preceding it.
55:7 says God set “ٱلْمِيزَانَ,” the balance. This makes ordered measure itself visible beside the source-section’s measured crafting and assigned shares.
55:8 commands not to transgress the balance, giving the source-section’s measure a moral boundary rather than leaving it as technique alone.
55:9 commands people to establish weight with justice and not diminish the balance. It completes the balance passage as a concrete ethical counterpart to measuring and dividing shares.
83:1 condemns those who give short measure. It supplies a specific ethical reversal of the source-section’s careful measurement before cutting and its allotted shares.
83:2 describes sellers who take full measure from others. It specifies one side of the double standard in 83:1–3, clarifying the abuse against which proper measure stands.
83:3 says they give less when measuring or weighing for others. It completes the reversal of careful measure: the tool of allotment is manipulated to deprive another.
5:91 says gambling breeds enmity and blocks remembrance of God and prayer. It completes 5:90 by showing what the source-section’s forbidden lot-game does to relations and worship.
6:2 joins creation from clay to a decreed term. The source-section’s definition of ق د ر as a thing’s extent and endpoint makes this a specific instance of creation bounded by a term.
82:8 says God composed the human in whatever form He willed. Following 82:7, it adds the chosen form to the source-section’s image of measuring, shaping, and preparing an object.
32:7 says God made good everything He created. This fits the source-section’s shaped-arrow image as purposeful workmanship, though the verse describes creation broadly.
16:9 says God’s is the direction of the way, while some ways are crooked. The source-section’s bent stick made straight and arrow guided toward a target give this contrast a concrete shape.

17:9 says the Qur’an guides to what is most upright. The source-section links ه د ي to an arrowhead aimed forward and س و ي to straightening what is crooked; this verse joins those two ideas in a guided, upright way.
1:6 asks God to guide the speaker to the straight path. This gives a direct route to the source-section’s arrow-point image of guidance, although the verse does not describe a crafted object.

6:136 describes people assigning shares of crops and livestock between God and their partners. It is a concrete human division of provision that contrasts with the source-section’s measured share from the Lord.
92:5 begins the giving-and-fearing route that leads to ease in 92:7. It parallels the source-section’s successful, purified choice and helps specify who is being eased.
92:6 says the giver affirms the best, completing the disposition before 92:7’s ease. It clarifies that the source-section’s direction is tied to response, not chance.
92:8 introduces the miser who feels self-sufficient, the opposite disposition to 92:5 and a concrete version of the source-section’s preference for worldly life.
92:9 says this person denies the best, explaining the turning away that leads to hardship in 92:10 and echoes 87:11.
92:11 says wealth will not avail when its owner falls. It qualifies the source-section’s worldly shares with the limit that a game’s or life’s wealth cannot secure the final outcome.
16:96 says what people possess ends while what is with God remains. It sharpens the source-section’s worn waterskin and its statement that the Hereafter is more abiding.
28:60 calls worldly gifts enjoyment and says what is with God is better and more lasting. This directly clarifies the source-section’s choice between the near life and the abiding one.

42:36 likewise contrasts worldly enjoyment with what remains with God. Its description of the enduring portion makes the source-section’s better, lasting afterlife a concrete counterweight to a worldly share.

57:20 compares worldly life to vegetation that grows after rain then dries and becomes debris. It makes passing worldly provision visible beside the source-section’s worn vessel and the claim that the Hereafter remains.

17:83 says that when a person receives favor, he turns away and withdraws, using نَأَىٰ بِجَانِبِهِ. The source-section’s root ج ن ب names both the two sides of a vessel and avoiding the reminder; this verse joins the side-word to turning away from favor.

41:51 repeats that upon favor a person “نَأَىٰ بِجَانِبِهِ” and turns aside. It makes the source-section’s ج ن ب branch for keeping away concrete as a response to provision, not just a vessel’s sides.

14:17 describes death approaching the person from every side in torment, yet he does not die. This is a specific fire-boundary parallel to 87:12–13 and clarifies the source-section’s line about neither dying nor living.

35:36 says the disbelievers in Hell are not put to death and their punishment is not lightened. This parallels the condition after the source-section’s great fire, though it states the death boundary rather than its full “nor live” wording.
